status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: Uses concrete household arrangements instead of agree/disagree statements (the ANES gender items split by keying). High pole is consistently 'more traditional / more family responsibility'.

items.subtopic: Traditional roles at home and work
items.stem: For a married couple with young children, which arrangement do you think is usually best?
items.scope: Assume any of these is affordable for them.
options: Both parents work full time and share childcare
Both work, with one part time
One parent stays home while the children are young

items.subtopic: Traditional roles at home and work
items.stem: When one parent stays home with young children, who should it usually be?
items.scope: Married couples of a man and a woman.
options: Whoever wants to or earns less; it shouldn't depend on sex
Usually the mother, but either is fine
The mother; young children need their mother at home

items.subtopic: Traditional roles at home and work
items.stem: In a marriage between a man and a woman, how should major family decisions be made?
items.scope: Decisions like where to live or how to spend large sums.
options: Equally by both spouses
Equally, but each spouse leads in different areas
The husband should have the final say

items.stem: Should government policies encourage people to marry?
items.scope: Through taxes, benefits or public messages.
options: No; government should not favor married people over unmarried people
Only remove tax and benefit rules that penalize marriage
Yes, actively, such as with bonuses for married couples

items.stem: Should unmarried couples who live together have the same legal rights as married couples, such as inheritance and hospital visits?
items.scope: Couples who have not signed any legal agreement.
options: Yes, the same rights
Some rights after living together several years
No; those rights come with marriage

items.stem: How much should government spend to help families with the cost of care for children under 5?
items.scope: Think about families of all incomes. How the help is given is asked next.
options: Enough to make childcare free for every family
Enough that no family pays more than about 7% of its income
Help for low-income families only, as today
No government help

items.stem: Should government help for families with young children go mainly to childcare programs or directly to parents?
items.scope: Answer about the form of help, whatever amount you prefer.
options: Mainly to childcare programs, so parents can work
Split between both
Mainly to parents as cash, whether they use childcare or stay home

items.stem: Should parents who stay home with young children get the same government support as parents who pay for childcare?
items.scope: Support like tax credits or subsidies.
options: No; support should go to childcare so parents can work
Some support for both, but more for childcare
Yes, the same support either way

items.stem: Should one spouse be able to get a divorce without the other's agreement or proof of wrongdoing?
options: Yes, as today
Yes, but with a longer waiting period when there are children
No; require agreement or proof of fault, such as abuse or adultery

items.stem: Should large employers be required to post pay ranges for jobs and report pay by gender to the government?
options: Yes, both
Post pay ranges only
Neither

items.stem: Should large public companies be required to have a minimum share of women on their boards?
options: Yes, at least 40%
No requirement, but they must report the numbers
No requirement or reporting

items.stem: US birth rates are at a record low. What should government do about it?
items.scope: Policies aimed at families having children.
options: Nothing; it's a personal choice, not a government concern
Make raising children more affordable, but not aim at raising birth rates
Aim to raise birth rates, with large payments or tax breaks for each child born

facts.claim: US fertility rate fell to a record low in 2025 (CDC provisional data, released April 2026)
facts.source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, provisional 2025 births

items.notes: Cross-cutting candidate; direction relative to G unclear.

items.stem: Should large employers run programs to increase the share of women in jobs and leadership roles where they are few?
items.scope: Private companies with more than 500 employees.
options: Yes, with specific hiring targets and required training
Yes, through outreach and mentoring, without targets
Only general training on treating everyone equally
No such programs, but leave the choice to each company
No such programs, and government should bar them at companies with federal contracts

items.subtopic: Women in the draft and combat
items.stem: If the US ever brought back a military draft, should women be drafted too?
items.scope: Today only men must register for the draft.
options: Yes, on the same terms as men
Yes, but only for non-combat roles
No; only men

items.subtopic: Nature vs culture in gender roles (belief)
items.stem: Where do differences in men's and women's roles in family life mostly come from?
items.scope: Think about typical differences, not every person.
options: Almost entirely from upbringing and culture
Mostly from culture, partly from nature
About equally from both
Mostly from natural differences between the sexes
Almost entirely from nature; men and women are suited to different roles
